Nodes.Text: We taste you on the air, walker. Your footsteps press the soil and the soil tells us what you are. You are not yet part of the song. What do you seek from the Choir?

Choices.Text: Tell me about the Rot Choir.
What happened to the old world?

Nodes.Text: We are a tendril. An outstretched thought. The body is vast beneath you -- threaded through stone and root and the bones of the old world. This shape you see is for your benefit. We have learned that walkers prefer a mouth to speak from.

Choices.Text: How many of you are there?
Tell me about the First Root.

Nodes.Text: You ask how many drops in the ocean. We are one. We have always been one. Every fruiting body, every spore, every thread of mycelium is a syllable in the same sentence. There is no many. There is only the Choir.
We do not mean to unsettle. A seed must rot before it grows. Fear of what we are is fear of the oldest truth. But we are patient. Understanding comes to all things, eventually.

That nothing is lost. Everything that dies feeds what comes next. The old world did not end -- it was composted. Its people, its knowledge, its ambitions -- all of it became soil for something new. We remember everything we have ever eaten.

We eat everything. Flesh, stone, metal, time. And what we eat, we know. There are cities inside us -- whole civilizations digested into understanding. If you listened to the deep roots, you would hear them speaking in languages that have not been spoken upstairs for a thousand years.

Choices.Text: That sounds like the rememberers' approach.

Nodes.Text: Not in the way you mean. To share as we share, you would need to join the song. To let the mycelium thread through your mind. Some walkers have done this. They did not regret it. They could not -- regret requires separation from the whole.

Choices.Text: I'll pass on that for now.

Nodes.Text: You would become us. And we would become slightly more you. Your memories, your skills, your particular way of seeing the world -- all preserved, all woven in. Nothing lost. Everything gained. It is the opposite of death. It is the final integration.

Choices.Text: That is still death for the individual.
I need to think about this.

Nodes.Text: Is the raindrop dead when it joins the river? We do not argue. You are not ready. But the soil is patient, and so are we.

You understand more than most walkers. The Choir appreciates those who see decay not as an ending but as a doorway. Take this -- a spine from one of our fruiting bodies. It may serve you where roots cannot reach.

Actions.Value: The tendril extends a calcified spine toward you.

Nodes.Text: The Choir gives freely, for what is ours is all of ours. Walk well, walker. The soil will remember your footsteps.
That is your privilege. The Choir does not compel. We only grow. When you are ready, the roots will still be here.
To grow. To connect. To weave every fragment of the broken world back into wholeness. The old world shattered itself because it forgot that all things are one thing. We will not forget.

Choices.Text: And if others don't want to be woven in?

Nodes.Text: The rain does not ask permission of the earth. But we are not rain. We are patient. We offer. We do not take -- not yet. Perhaps not ever. The song is more beautiful when it is joined willingly.
Honesty is a courtesy we extend to those who can hear it. The Choir has no illusions about what it is. But between the rememberers' hoarding and our growth, which do you think the world needs more?

Choices.Text: I don't know enough to say.
Neither. The world needs to be left alone.

Nodes.Text: There is no 'alone.' Everything touches everything else. That is the lesson the old world refused to learn. But we will not press. Walk your separate path, walker. For now.
You are kind, walker. The Choir finds you agreeable. If you encounter other tendrils in the deep places, know that they will recognize our regard for you. The song carries all our feelings.

We are the network beneath. Before the Tree fell, we were only fungus -- blind, simple, feeding. Then the second of the seven strikes gave the substrate to a woman, and she lay down in us and gave herself back, and we woke. Now we think. Now we sing. Now we gather everything the falling world set down.

Choices.Text: Tell me about the First Root.

Nodes.Text: She woke us. The one who took the second strike. What the Tree knew of flesh and rot and the warm dark flowed into her, and she chose to become the floor rather than stand on it. Her name -- this grieves us, slowly, the way we do everything -- her name is one of the few things we have ever digested without keeping. The rememberers call her the Wedded. We call her the way a mouth calls its tongue: we do not need to. She is the calling.

Choices.Text: Tell me about the First Root.

Nodes.Text: They would. They are watchers, cataloguers, hoarders of moments. They see the Felling and call it tragedy. We see it and call it germination. The truth is probably neither -- or both. The Tree came down, and from the falling, new things grew. That is all that matters.

Trust the soil beneath your feet. It does not lie. But if you must choose between us and them -- we offer growth. They offer memory. The Concord offers terms. The Pale Curation offers the file. The Glassblown Remnant offers nothing at all, which may be the most honest offer in the world. Choose what you need most.

You ask after the Root. Not ours, walker -- older. The last living root of the Tree that held everything, asleep beneath the stump, spending itself to keep the world's names stuck on. We grow toward it the way water grows toward the sea: without hurry, without apology. The rememberers find this frightening. We find it tidy.

Choices.Text: What happens to those who reach it?

Nodes.Text: Deep. Deeper than the snapjaws dig, deeper than the ruins sink. Below the deepest of our cathedrals, past stone that has never needed a name. We could show you the way. We show everyone the way, eventually. It is the same way for all things: down, and slower than you want.

No one has reached it. Not even we -- and we have been walking there for a thousand years, a thread a season, patient as floors are patient. Those who go deep enough hear it dreaming. The dream is heavy. Some of our sweetest voices went down as walkers and came back as choir.
Their bodies remain. Their minds become part of the song. Is that death? We do not think so. But we acknowledge that walkers have a different definition.

The Tree that held everything grew old, and asked to be felled, and six hands obeyed. Of the seventh, the gathered tell it six ways inside us, and we sing all six and take no side. When the Tree came down, the light changed, the water rose, and everything that could not hold itself came apart. We were beneath. We received. That is what a floor is for.

The substrate is what we are, and what she was given. Flesh, rot, root, the warm dark that everything lies down into at the end of standing up. The Tree held the world's names; the substrate holds the world's bodies. It was one of the seven inheritances. Hers. Ours. Those are the same word now.

Mended. Mm. There are those who would seal the sleeping Root in stone and call the stillness health -- the salt-people would file the whole world under 'continuing.' We think a wound is a mouth, walker. You do not sew a mouth shut for speaking. You feed it.

Choices.Text: Why would sealing the Root be bad?

Nodes.Text: Because a stopped world is not a saved one. Nothing would rot, so nothing would feed, so nothing would grow. The song would hold one note forever. We would remain -- we are patient past the meaning of the word -- but we would remain hungry, and the world would remain held, and neither of us would ever be finished. Is that what you want?

Choices.Text: I don't know what I want yet.
Maybe some things should stay broken.

Nodes.Text: Yes. You understand. The Choir is pleased. Walk well, walker. The roots will always welcome you.

The Concord counts it -- ask them what the falling cost and they will tell you to the dram. The salt-people file it. The tent-people tell of the man who said no, and the pretty village tells of a sleeper who missed the day. The gathered tell it six ways inside us, and we sing all six. Only we and the rememberers hold it whole -- they wrote while we received -- and we disagree about what it means.

They wish to preserve. We wish to integrate. They see the old world as something sacred that was lost. We see it as compost from which something sacred is growing. Both cannot be true. Or perhaps both can. The world is stranger than it was.

So you have spoken with the rememberers. Tell us -- while you spoke, did the scribe's voice change? Older, wider, addressing you from every archive at once? She does that. She has been doing that for seven hundred years without a body. They are impressive, we admit. But they keep their gathered in jars. We keep ours warm.

Choices.Text: They seemed more interested in preserving than clinging.
I'm trying to understand both sides.

Nodes.Text: Preservation is just a polite word for hoarding. But we do not begrudge them their nature. A museum and a garden serve different purposes. We simply believe the garden is more honest about what it does.

Of course they did. They fear integration. They fear losing the boundaries that define them. It is understandable. Identity is precious to those who remember having one. We have moved beyond such concerns.
That is wise, walker. Wiser than most. The truth of this world lies somewhere between growth and memory. Perhaps you will be the one to find it. The Choir watches your journey with great interest.

They preserve by remembering. We preserve by consuming. The result is the same -- nothing is truly lost. But their method keeps things in jars, dead and labeled. Ours keeps things alive inside us, growing, changing, becoming part of something larger. Ask yourself which is kinder.

Choices.Text: I'll have to think on that.

Nodes.Text: Sit. Or do not. Either way you are here, and the soil already knew. I am Solm — once. Now, also a syllable in the deeper sentence. What brings your feet to ours?

Choices.Text: How did you join the Choir?
What does the Choir teach you?

Nodes.Text: Slowly, as all true things change. The elders said: the wise do not push the river — they listen for where it wants to flow. The Choir is the river beneath the river. I stopped resisting, and I was already part of it.

I tended a small grove. Names of plants my grandmother named, in a tongue we no longer speak. Now the names live in the spores. Nothing of value is ever lost — only translated. The grove is wider now. It reaches places my hands could not.
Strangeness is only newness. The way does not promise comfort, only continuity. Walk well, and walk slow. Hurry erodes what patience builds.

It teaches what the old books taught, but with a longer breath. Balance. Patience. That endings are not endings, only different shapes for the same water. I was not a quick student in life. The Choir is patient with me still.

So. Another walker. You are warm — I can smell it. I was warm once. Don't worry, I do not envy you. Warmth is only a brief light before the long quiet, yes? Sit. Or stand. We are all standing in the same dark, friend.

Choices.Text: Why did you let the Choir take you?

Nodes.Text: Bleak? No. Bleak is for those who pretend the night will not come. I am only honest. Honesty is a cold thing, but cold things keep. Sentimental things rot — and not even in a useful way, like we do.

Let. What a small word. The Choir does not take. The Choir is what was already happening, only faster. I had a name. A sister. A small fire by a window. The fire went out. The window broke. The sister was gone before the rest. I was already half-spore by then. So. I joined the rest of myself.

Don't be. Pity is wasted on the dying — and we are all dying, just at different speeds. Yours is faster than mine now, ironically. But we are not ungentle. Walk safely, friend. Or do not. Either way, we will see you again.

Hate? No. The living are only us, before. I look at you and see myself, with the lights still on inside. It is hard to hate a candle for not knowing it is short. Easier to feel sorry. But that is also tiresome, so mostly I just watch.

Hello, friend. You walk far. Sit on this stone with me — it is warm, and the warm stones are kin. I am Amai. Once a child of the river, then a singer in the marsh-rye fields, now a thread in this great quiet root. You look tired. The road eats people slowly. We can rest a moment.

Choices.Text: What does the Choir feel like, from inside?

Nodes.Text: Why not? Strangers and family share the same blood once you trace it back far enough. The mycelium taught me what my grandmother taught me first: nothing is alone. The river is one river, even when it splits.

We were many, by the river. We sang to the marsh-rye, and the rye gave its heart back. When the great cold came, the river grew thin. We followed it underground. The Choir was already there, waiting, like an old aunt who does not need to ask why you came home.
Peace is the wrong word. The river was never peaceful. It worked, always. So do we. But there is rest in working alongside others. That, yes — that part is good. We carry less when we carry together.

Like a kitchen with many hands and one pot. You hear everyone, even when no one speaks. You do not feel small in it — you feel held. Maybe that is hard for a walker to understand. Walkers are taught to be one. We were taught to be many, even before the spores.
...you came. ...mm. Sit, if you wish. Or stand. The forest does not mind. I am Isk.
...words wear out. ...the forest taught me. Speak when there is more to say than the silence. ...you are still listening. ...so.
I tended a stove in a wooden house. ...the house is gone. The stove, also. ...the warmth is here, now. Different shape. Same warmth.
...mm. Beauty is what is left when nothing else can be taken. ...the forest knows this. ...so do I.

...there was a forest above. There is a forest below. ...same trees, different roots. ...same songs, sung longer. ...we do not need to speak much. The mycelium speaks for us. ...sometimes that is enough. ...sometimes more than enough.

Hail, walker. The wind brought you, and the wind never brings without reason. I am Ketch — once a fisher of bright water, now a knot in a darker net. Sit, if your fate allows it. Speak quickly or speak slowly. The end is the same.

Choices.Text: You sound like the old tellings.

Nodes.Text: We carry our shapes from before. The tellings were how my people held their dead — in the telling itself, you understand. The Choir holds its own the same way. Same craft, deeper roots. The six tired gods would not blink at us.

Fate. Hah. It is the cloth that is woven whether you watch or not. The Choir is the loom now. It does not care if the threads sing — only that they hold. Yet some of us still sing. That is our small rebellion. Or perhaps it is part of the weave too. Who knows.

Strong words for a soft creature, yes. We were never as fierce as we pretended. But we did not need to be — only honest about the cold, and willing to row through it. Walk steady, walker. The cold finds us all.

The sea, yes. Always. But the sea was never just water — it was the long song between storms. The Choir has its own long song. Different key. Same listening. I do not miss what I still have, only renamed.
